paper_title: Residual Guidance for Real-Time Interactive Video Generation

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Real-time interactive video generation allows users to change the prompt during generation to steer the evolving video. However, existing streaming models, which generate videos chunk by chunk, often keep following the previous prompt after a switch. We trace this failure to context inertia, where the previous chunk acts as a strong prior that suppresses the new prompt. Furthermore, we find that this inertia persists even when the cache retains only the previous chunk, yet discarding the context breaks visual continuity, which limits approaches that edit the cache. Rather than editing the cache, we propose Residual Guidance (RG), a simple, training-free method that counteracts context inertia with a correction measured outside the cache. Specifically, RG denoises the re-noised previous chunk once under the new prompt without the cache and adds the resulting residual to the early denoising steps of the next chunk, where its content is largely decided and the new prompt is most suppressed. Across settings ranging from a single switch to long multi-switch generation, RG substantially improves prompt switching capability on existing streaming models, including those with dedicated switching mechanisms, while largely retaining visual quality. As it requires no training or per-model tuning and adds only one forward pass per chunk, RG can be easily integrated into existing real-time video generation pipelines.

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Real-time interactive video generation allows users to change the prompt during generation to steer the evolving video. However, existing streaming models, which generate videos chunk by chunk, often keep following the previous prompt after switch. We trace this failure to context inertia, where the previous chunk acts as strong prior that suppresses the new prompt. Furthermore, we find that this inertia persists even when the cache retains only the previous chunk, yet discarding the context breaks visual continuity, which limits approaches that edit the cache. Rather than editing the cache, we propose Residual Guidance (RG), simple, training-free method that counteracts context inertia with correction measured outside the cache. Specifically, RG denoises the re-noised previous chunk once under the new prompt without the cache and adds the resulting residual to the early denoising steps of the next chunk, where its content is largely decided and the new prompt is most suppressed. Across settings ranging from single switch to long multi-switch generation, RG substantially improves prompt switching capability on existing streaming models, including those with dedicated switching mechanisms, while largely retaining visual quality. As it requires no training or per-model tuning and adds only one forward pass per chunk, RG can be easily integrated into existing real-time video generation pipelines. 1 1. Introduction Conventional video diffusion models [13, 18, 27, 31, 40, 51, 58, 61, 62] typically employ bidirectional attention, allowing video tokens to attend to both past and future frames. Consequently, they generate predefined sequence of frames jointly, with the prompt specified before generation and the video becoming available only after the entire sequence has been denoised. This prevents users from interacting with the generation process as the video unfolds. Recent autoregressive video diffusion models instead adopt causal attention [6], where each chunk attends to previous chunks through KV cache [41]. Combined with few-step distillation from bidirectional teacher [9, 19, 26, 34, 56, 60, 63], such models achieve real-time streaming generation, in which each chunk is displayed as soon as it is generated. Since the video unfolds while it is being generated, users can change the prompt along the way to steer the evolving video [22, 33, 43, 47, 56, 57, 59], for example, to introduce new event, modify an existing scene, or control simulated environment. However, this interaction remains unreliable. As shown in Fig. 1 and Fig. 2a, streaming models often fail to reflect prompt changes and continue to generate content consistent with the previous prompt. Existing approaches modify the KV cache at prompt boundaries to improve responsiveness [56, 59], yet the problem persists. To understand this failure, we analyze the models prediction of the switch chunk (Fig. 2b) and find that the cached visual content acts as strong prior that suppresses the new prompt, phenomenon we term context inertia. Our analysis reveals two properties of context inertia. First, the inertia comes from what the cached frames depict rather than from the prompt used to generate them, and persists even when only the previous chunk is cached. This explains why cache-based approaches fall short, as re-caching [56] updates only the prompt information while keeping the cached frames, and flushing the cache [59] still retains the sink and the last frame. Second, the suppression is most pronounced at the first denoising step, where the content of the chunk is largely determined. Removing the context entirely would eliminate the inertia but would break subject identity and scene continuity (Fig. 2c), suggesting that the cache should be kept and its pull countered in the prediction instead. natural way to do so is classifier-free guidance [17], but its direction is computed under the same cache and is likewise suppressed (see Supp. F.2). Together, these observations suggest that the prompt signal should be measured without the cache, where context inertia is absent, and applied where the inertia is strongest. Based on this insight, we propose Residual Guidance (RG), simple, training-free method that strengthens the new prompt without cache modification. Specifically, RG denoises re-noised copy of the preceding chunk under the new prompt without the cache and adds its difference from the original chunk to the early denoising steps of the next chunk. This residual captures how the previous content would be redrawn under the new prompt without context inertia, releasing the prediction from that content and supplying the suppressed prompt signal. Because the correction acts on the prediction rather than on the cache, each chunk still attends to its full context, which preserves subject identity and scene continuity. For the same reason, RG is orthogonal to how the cache is managed and can be combined with existing cache-based switching methods. RG requires only one additional forward pass per chunk and uses single configuration across models. We evaluate our approach on seven streaming baselines, including methods with dedicated switching mechanisms, across settings ranging from single switch in 5 video to six prompts over 60 s. RG improves average switch achievement from 21% to 58% on single-attribute switches, from 47% to 66% on three-event stories, and from 66% to 81% on long interactive generation, while largely preserving visual quality. The improvements hold across all baselines and persist over successive switches. In user study, RG achieves an overall preference score of 70.7%. RG reduces throughput by only 6% in the single-switch setting, making it practical for real-time generation. Our contributions are summarized as follows: (1) We characterize context inertia in streaming video generation, showing that cached visual content, rather than stale prompt information, suppresses new prompts, particularly at the first denoising step. (2) We propose Residual Guidance, simple, training-free method that counteracts context inertia in the prediction rather than in the cache, by measuring the effect of the new prompt without the cache and applying it where the inertia is strongest. (3) We demonstrate its effectiveness on seven streaming baselines across diverse switching scenarios, with consistent gains in prompt-switch responsiveness at minimal cost in quality and speed. 2. Related Work Prompt switching in real-time video generation. Recent streaming models distill bidirectional teachers into few-step causal students [9, 19, 26, 34, 56, 60, 63] that condition each chunk on previously generated content through KV cache [41]. To handle prompt switches, LongLive [56] attributes the failure to stale prompt information in the cache and re-encodes past frames under the new prompt, while Infinity-RoPE [59] keeps only sink and the last frame and Anchor Forcing [57] rebuilds the cache from stored anchor states. MemFlow [22] and SWIFT [47] instead manage the memory by retrieving prompt-relevant history and injecting transition-aware signals, respectively. Despite their different memory strategies, these methods all retain previously generated visual content in the cache, which we find continues to suppress the new prompt 2 (a) (b) (c) Figure 2. Even single cached chunk suppresses it. (c) Chunks generated under each context (columns) for the same switch. The white bear persists with the full or previous-chunk context, partially darkens with the oldest chunk only, and turns black without context at the cost of identity and background. (Sec. 3). RG instead counteracts this suppression in the prediction rather than in the cache, which preserves continuity and keeps it compatible with these approaches. Guidance in video generation. Classifier-free guidance (CFG) [17] strengthens conditioning by extrapolating the conditional prediction away from the unconditional one and is widely used in video diffusion models [13, 51, 58]. Streaming students, however, are distilled at fixed guidance scale [60], and applying CFG on top of this distilled guidance only partially restores prompt responsiveness. Its two branches are computed under the same cache, so the guidance direction is suppressed along with the prompt, and larger scales introduce artifacts (Supp. F.2). History Guidance [45] combines predictions across history conditions, enabled by its frame-wise noise-level training, to improve temporal consistency rather than prompt responsiveness. MAGI-1 [49] uses separate history and text guidance scales, but only its non-distilled model exposes an independently adjustable text guidance. In contrast, RG measures cache-free prediction with an already generated chunk, so its direction is not suppressed by the context, and it requires no unconditional branch. detailed comparison is provided in Supp. F.1. Diffusion-based editing. Many diffusionand flow-based editing methods derive editing signals from source-target prediction differences. Delta Denoising Score [16] and Contrastive Denoising Score [38] use denoising prediction differences, while DreamMotion [21] uses score distillation with space-time self-similarity constraints. Delta Rectified Flow Sampling [4] extends delta-based guidance to velocity fields. FlowEdit [28] transports between source and target distributions, and FlowDirector [29] uses ODEbased flow corrections. ProxEdit [14] regularizes sourcetarget differences, while TurboEdit [10] and ChordEdit [35] enable few-step and one-step image editing, respectively. StreamEdit [23] also builds on few-step streaming video generators without training, but edits source video by conditioning dual-branch sampler on it, whereas RG has no source video and counteracts the cached context of the ongoing generation. SDEdit [36] simply re-noises an input and reconstructs it for image editing. RG also re-noises the preceding chunk, but applies the difference between its cache-free reconstruction and the original chunk to the next chunk, without requiring the previous prompt or inversion. 3. Context Inertia Notation. streaming model generates video autoregressively in units of one or more latent frames, referred to as chunks. We denote the clean latent of chunk by sk and its noisy state at noise level by xt = αtsk + σtϵ. Chunk is denoised in few steps t1 > t2 > > tQ (typically = 4) by student denoiser ˆxθ, which predicts the clean chunk from its noisy state, conditioned on prompt yk and causal KV cache C<k storing keyvalue states computed from preceding chunks s1, . . . , sk1. We denote this prediction by ˆxθ(xt C<k, yk), or simply ˆx(C, y) for fixed noisy input. prompt switch occurs at chunk when the prompt changes from yold = yk1 to ynew = yk = yold. We call chunk the switch chunk, so that sk1 is the last chunk generated under yold. 3.1. Prompt Switches Are Rarely Reflected We analyze Self Forcing [19], representative causal streaming student whose rolling KV cache is retained across the switch, and LongLive [56], an interactive model that recomputes cached states under the new prompt at prompt boundaries. We build development set of 100 switch pairs (yold, ynew) with an LLM [39], covering diverse changes (e.g., color and motion), where yold and ynew describe the states before and after the change. For each pair, we generate 10 video of 14 chunks with the switch at 5 s, leaving 7 chunks to reflect the new prompt. VLM [1] then judges whether each post-switch chunk reflects ynew. We categorize switch as immediate if ynew appears within the first 2 chunks after the switch (about 1.5 s, allowing one chunk for 3 smooth transition), delayed if it appears in later chunk, and never if it does not appear within the video. As shown in Fig. 2a, only 16% and 25% of switches are immediate for Self Forcing and LongLive, respectively, while 80% and 64% are never realized. Supp. A.1 details the prompt construction and VLM evaluation, and Supp. A.2 reports the results by type of prompt change. 3.2. Why Do Prompt Switches Fail? To isolate the effects of the prompt and the context, we run the model unchanged up to the switch chunk and fix its noisy input xt at each denoising step. From this fixed input, we compute ˆx(C, y) under visible context C<k, restricted by hiding cached keys from self-attention, where = hides all of them. We measure the prompt response as the displacement induced by switching from yold to ynew, normalized by the same displacement without context: ρ(C) = ˆx(C, ynew) ˆx(C, yold) ˆx(, ynew) ˆx(, yold) , (1) so that ρ(C) is the fraction of the context-free prompt response retained under C, with ρ() = 1. For the numerator, since the cache may carry information about the prompt under which it was built, we recache LongLive under ynew, so that the suppression cannot be attributed to stale prompt information. For the denominator, = reproduces the context-free setting of the first chunk of every video, which keeps the evaluation in distribution. Finding 1: The context suppresses the prompt. We examine how the cached context affects the response to the new prompt, both quantitatively and qualitatively. Unless otherwise noted, we report ρ at the first denoising step, which we show below to be the most affected. As shown in Fig. 2b, at the first denoising step the full context retains only 0.18 and 0.27 of the context-free prompt response for Self Forcing and LongLive, respectively, suppression of the new prompt by cached content that we refer to as context inertia. Furthermore, with the previous chunk alone, ρ reaches only 0.28 and 0.42 for the two models, and even with the oldest chunk alone it stays at 0.59 and 0.53, far below 1. single recent chunk thus accounts for most of the suppression, and even distant frames contribute. Since LongLive is measured after recaching, this suppression stems largely from the cached visual content itself rather than stale prompt information. The generated chunks in Fig. 2c exhibit the same trend: the white bear persists under the full context or the previous chunk alone and only partially darkens with the oldest chunk. Removing the context entirely finally produces the black bear, but at the cost of its identity and background, since the chunk is then determined solely by the noise and the prompt. One might expect stronger classifier-free guidance to counteract this suppression. Since the guidance direction ˆx(C, ynew) ˆx(C, y), where denotes the empty prompt, is computed under the same cache, it is suppressed as well, and larger guidance scale mainly amplifies artifacts rather than restoring the prompt response (Supp. F.2). Finding 2: Context inertia is strongest at the first step. To see where along the few-step trajectory this suppression arises, we repeat the measurement at every denoising step and find that two distinct effects both peak at the first step: the prompt alone moves the prediction most, and the context suppresses this movement most. First, without context, the change in the clean prediction of the switch chunk induced by switching from yold to ynew, ˆx(, ynew) ˆx(, yold)/sk1, is 0.62 at step 1 for Self Forcing, but only 0.19 at step 2 and 0.03 at step 4. Second, with context, the fraction of this response that survives, ρ, is lowest at step 1, and the response lost there is not recovered at later steps (see Supp. A.3 for details). We attribute both to the coarseto-fine nature of diffusion sampling, where early high-noise steps largely determine layout and content while later steps refine details [3, 7, 15], an effect likely amplified in few-step students whose first step covers most of the noise range. 4. Method Sec. 3 suggests that following the new prompt requires evaluating it without the cache, whereas preserving visual continuity requires generating with it. Residual Guidance (RG) satisfies both by measuring the prompt signal without the cache while generating the chunk with it. Specifically, RG reconstructs re-noised copy of the preceding chunk under the new prompt without the cache, and adds its residual from the original chunk to the cache-conditioned prediction of the next chunk at the early denoising steps, where context inertia is strongest. 4.1. Posterior View of the Problem The intuition above has simple probabilistic interpretation. The clean prediction of the student approximates the posterior mean of sk given its noisy state xt k, the preceding cache C<k, and the prompt ynew. Since the forward noising process does not depend on the prompt (i.e., xt ynew sk, C<k), this posterior factorizes as p(sk xt k, C<k, ynew) p(sk xt k, C<k) p(ynew sk, C<k). (2) The first term favors continuing the cached content, and the second favors the new prompt. Context inertia arises when the first term dominates the second. Methods that edit the cache at switch [56, 59] weaken the first term, and stronger text guidance amplifies the second, yet this term is still computed under the cache, so much of the suppression remains. RG instead adds residual measured without the cache, which pushes the prediction toward the new prompt and away from the cached content. Both effects contribute to the gain (Tab. 3). At the same time, since the chunk is still generated under the full cache, visual continuity with the preceding chunks is largely retained. 4.2. Residual Guidance Residual estimation. To measure the effect of the new prompt without context inertia, the preceding chunk sk1 is first re-noised to noise level τ and then denoised in single step under ynew without the KV cache: xτ k1 = ατ sk1 + στ ϵ, rk = ˆxθ(xτ k1 , ynew) sk1. ϵ (0, I), (3) Here, denotes an empty KV cache, so the preceding chunk enters the reconstruction only through its re-noised latent. The residual measures how the cache-free reconstruction under ynew differs from the original chunk, and part of it is independent of ynew, counteracting the previous content itself. It is thus not an exact estimate of the prompt term in Eq. (2) but an approximate correction to the cache-conditioned prediction (see Supp. B.1). The noise level τ , chosen independently of the sampling steps ti, sets how much of the preceding chunk the reconstruction retains and thus the strength of the correction, analogous to the guidance scale in classifier-free guidance [17]. Residual injection. The residual rk is measured on chunk 1 and applied to chunk k. Context inertia itself motivates this transfer. Since the cache-conditioned prediction of chunk stays close to sk1, correction derived from sk1 also applies to it. The residual is added to the clean prediction at the early denoising steps: ˆx(i) = ˆxθ(xti C<k, ynew) + λirk, (4) with λ = (1, 0.5, 0, 0) over the four steps. The correction thus acts where the suppression is strongest (Sec. 3), while the remaining steps run unmodified under the full cache and keep the chunk consistent with its history. Unlike classifier-free guidance, which contrasts two predictions with the cache, the residual is measured without the cache and is therefore not attenuated by it. Implementation. For every chunk generated under ynew, the residual is recomputed from its preceding chunk, until the next prompt switch. We set τ = 850 for all models and sample ϵ once per switch, sharing it across the prompt interval (Supp. D.6). Alternative interventions, including residuals against the empty or previous prompt, partial cache removal, and stronger classifier-free guidance, yield smaller gains or degrade visual continuity (Supp. F.3). Both ablations and alternatives are examined in Sec. 5.3, and the full algorithm is given in Supp. B.2. 5. Experiments 5.1. Setup Baselines. We apply RG to Self Forcing [19], Causal Forcing [63], and MemFlow [22], which retain the cache at switches, to LongLive [56] and Infinity-RoPE [59], which modify the cache, and to Anchor Forcing [57] and SWIFT [47], which use dedicated switch mechanisms. Since RG leaves the cache untouched, it plugs into all seven baselines regardless of how they manage the cache, without retraining or per-model tuning, using the same configuration throughout. All are distilled from Wan2.1-1.3B [51], generate 832 480 videos, and use their native sampling. Each model and its RG variant share the same seed, ensuring identical pre-switch frames. We further apply our method to Rolling Forcing [34] in Supp. E.2. Datasets. We evaluate RG in three settings of increasing duration and number of switches, each probing different aspect of prompt switching. First, the 200 dynamic attribute prompts of T2V-CompBench [46] are split into initial and final states and generated as 5 videos with the switch at 2 s. Since only one attribute of the same subject changes, this setting most directly tests context inertia. Second, 100 three-event stories from StoryEval [53] are generated as 10 videos, with their events used as consecutive prompts and switches at 3 and 7 s, testing whether model can switch repeatedly. Third, following MemFlow [22] and other interactive methods [47, 56, 57], we use 100 scripts of six prompts, each active for 10 over 60 video, which we refer to as InteractiveBench. Prompt construction is detailed in Supp. C.1. Supp. E.1, E.3, and F.4 further cover actionbinding prompts, where new subject appears at the switch, InteractiveBench extended to 240 s, and explicit scene cuts with Infinity-RoPE [59] and its RoPE Cut. Metrics. VLM judge [1] determines whether the post-switch video depicts the new prompt (reliability in Supp. C.3). Achievement is the fraction of switches after which the video depicts the new prompt. We exclude new prompts that the model cannot render even as an initial prompt, so that failures reflect the switch rather than the prompt. On the post-switch segment, we report CLIP similarity [42] to the new prompt and the VBench [20] quality score, which aggregates seven quality dimensions with the official normalization and weights. We also report VBench dynamic degree, which ensures that consistency is not obtained simply by producing static videos. Conclusion In this work, we trace the failure of prompt switching in streaming video generation to context inertia: cached visual content suppresses the influence of new prompt, and existing cache-based switching strategies do not fully remove this suppression. Residual Guidance (RG) addresses the problem by measuring the effect of the new prompt without the cache and adding the resulting residual to the next chunk at its early denoising steps, where context inertia is strongest. RG needs no training, combines with existing switching methods, and adds only one forward pass per chunk, making it practical for real-time use. Across seven streaming baselines and settings ranging from single switch to multiple switches in long video generation, RG substantially improves switch achievement while retaining visual continuity. Nevertheless, some changes remain difficult, such as removing an object, and fine details can be altered along with the requested change. Evaluation Protocol C.1. Benchmarks and Prompt Construction Prompt Details. The prompts of T2V-CompBench dynamic attribute [46] describe change of attribute in single sentence, for example timelapse of leaf transitioning from green to bright red as autumn progresses. Therefore, we split each prompt into one for the initial state and one for the final state, with the subject and the setting kept fixed, for example yold green leaf on tree branch and ynew bright red leaf on tree branch. shared description of motion, lighting and camera is then appended to both prompts (e.g., . . . , swaying gently in the breeze, soft natural light, slow camera push-in). This description serves two purposes. First, bare description of state tends to yield nearly static video, whereas the appended description gives the scene ongoing motion that must continue across the switch, as in interactive use. Second, the streaming models are trained on long, detailed prompts, and the appended description keeps the inputs close to this distribution. Since the description is identical in yold and ynew, the two prompts differ only in the changed state, so any difference after the switch can be attributed to it. The split was performed with an LLM and checked manually by the authors. StoryEval [53] contains prompts with two to four events. Relation to Prior Work Relation to prior analyses. Several recent works report related forms of history-induced suppression, but approach them primarily through cache or memory design. LongLive [56] observes that retaining the KV cache delays or prevents prompt switches, attributes this to residual information from the previous prompt, and introduces KV recaching to address it. SWIFT [47] similarly identifies mismatch between cached video history and updated prompt semantics, and proposes semantic injection and adaptive memory allocation. Echo-Forcing [54] identifies interference from outdated scene memories and addresses it through structured scene memories and discrepancy-aware memory decay. In the related but distinct setting of actionconditioned world modeling, Astra [64] studies how longer visual histories reduce action responsiveness, refers to this phenomenon as visual inertia, and mitigates it through noise-augmented history memory. second line of work examines the denoising steps of autoregressive video diffusion under fixed prompt. Bai et al. [2] find that content and motion are largely established at the first denoising step and attribute this to the historical context. HiAR [65] relate the first step of few-step students to motion dynamics and sample diversity. In-Context Forcing [55] further shows that Self Forcing attends more strongly to the previous frame than to the current one at the first step, and links this to weakened dynamics. These studies focus on motion, diversity, or temporal drift rather than prompt-switch responsiveness, and primarily address their findings through student retraining. Our analysis complements both lines. We isolate how the visual content of the retained context suppresses promptinduced prediction changes, even after recaching under the new prompt. We further measure the prompt response at each denoising step and show that the step at which the prompt acts most strongly is also the step at which the context suppresses it most, so that later steps cannot recover the switch. The suppression is already substantial with single preceding chunk. Together, these findings identify where training-free correction should act, which motivates the design of RG. Relation to guidance-based methods. Tab. 13 compares residual guidance with the three guidance schemes that it most resembles, and all four can be written as correction added to the prediction of the switch chunk. The key distinction lies in the reference used to construct each correction: CFG and MAGI-1 measure prompt directions under cached context, History Guidance reinforces the context, whereas RG estimates the new-prompt displacement without cached context. Specifically, Classifier-free guidance [17] adds (w 1)[ˆx(C, y) ˆx(C, )], the prompt direction measured under the context, at every step. History guidance [45] adds (w 1)[ˆx(C, y) ˆx(, y)], the context direction, which strengthens the context rather than the prompt, and it requires model trained with history dropout so that ˆx(, y) is defined. MAGI-1 [49] combines both with separate scales, (wtext 1)[ˆx(C, y) ˆx(C, )]+(wprev 1)[ˆx(C, ) ˆx(, )], and raises wprev to reduce flicker between chunks, which strengthens exactly the context that suppresses switch. Its prompt direction is the same as in classifier-free guidance, measured under the context, and it is disabled in the distilled MAGI-1 since the student has no null prompt. Sec. 3.2 shows that this direction shrinks under the context, so that the scale required to realize switch saturates the prediction before the switch is reached. We discuss this more in Supp. F.2. Residual guidance differs in the quantity it adds. The direction rk = ˆx(, ynew) sk1 that we use is measured without the context and is therefore not rescaling of the prompt direction of CFG and MAGI-1, which is measured under the context. History guidance also evaluates context-free prediction, but on the current noisy sample and as the point to move away from, which reinforces the context, whereas RG evaluates it on the re-noised previous chunk and moves the prediction toward it. Its reference is the previous clean chunk rather than the current noisy sample, so it is computed once per chunk instead of at every step. Its magnitude is governed by the noise level τ , while its contribution at each denoising step is controlled by λi, rather than by CFG scale. The context-free query is obtained from the student itself, which runs without cache on the first chunk of every video, so no unconditional branch and no training are needed. F.2. Scene cuts Some prompts in our benchmarks already involve scene cut, as in film editing. For example, in Fig. 12, spilled water forms river and boat then sails on it. Here, we examine this setting directly with prompts that keep the subject and replace the entire scene. RG is applied to Infinity-RoPE with RoPE Cut enabled, which is its mechanism designed for scene cuts. As shown in Fig. 20, Infinity-RoPE often remains in the previous scene even with RoPE Cut, whereas RG moves to the new scene at each switch while retaining the subject.
